title: Backstop resources

definition.text: The theory that as a heavily used limited resource grows expensive, alternatives become cheap by comparison and so become worth using.

facts.text: In the long run it assumes technological progress will make backstop resources essentially unlimited, with need driving new technologies to become cost effective.
Examples include Canada developing tar sands after the 1979 oil price spike and South Africa turning coal into fuel under anti-apartheid embargoes.
Critics say it ignores the infrastructure alternatives need: a hydrogen car is easy compared with building a hydrogen supply network.

contested_note: Environmental economists dispute the theory's reliance on technology and its neglect of resource exploitation and infrastructure.

title: Cornucopianism

definition.text: The view that advancing technology can keep supplying humanity's material needs, so growth is practically unlimited.

facts.text: The name comes from the cornucopia, the horn of plenty of Greek mythology; cornucopians or boomsters are contrasted with Malthusian doomsters.
Julian Simon's 1981 book The Ultimate Resource argued that humans have always found ways to develop resources past nearly any roadblock.
Simon held that free markets are needed: when a resource's price rises because supply is short, research into cheaper alternatives follows.
The label is rarely self-applied and is mostly used critically by those who see the view as over-optimistic.
Naomi Oreskes argued that many key innovations came from government action and that technological progress has not stopped the climate crisis.

contested_note: Critics such as Lindsey Grant and Naomi Oreskes reject cornucopian arguments as flawed or over-optimistic.

title: Critical raw materials

definition.text: Raw materials that have no viable substitutes with current technology, that most consuming countries must import, and whose supply is dominated by one or a few producers.

facts.text: Criticality has no agreed definition and varies with time, country and context.
The European Commission's list grew from 14 critical raw materials in 2011 to 34 in 2023; they are mainly used in energy transition and digital technologies.
In 2023 Europe relied on China for 98% of its rare-earth needs and 97% of its lithium.
The EU's Critical Raw Materials Act, in force from 23 May 2024, aims by 2030 to extract at least 10%, process at least 40% and recycle at least 25% of EU annual consumption domestically.

notes: The Critical Raw Materials Act itself is an EU law; folded in here rather than given its own entry.

definition.text: The apparent link between a boom in one sector, such as natural resources, and a decline in other sectors such as manufacturing or agriculture.

facts.text: The Economist coined the term in 1977 for the decline of Dutch manufacturing after the Groningen gas field was discovered in 1959.
Boom revenues strengthen the country's currency, making its other exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper, so those sectors lose competitiveness.
It can follow any large inflow of foreign currency, including foreign aid and foreign direct investment, not just resource discoveries.
Trade theory says resource-rich countries should specialise in extraction, but this can backfire when resources deplete, since manufacturing cannot return as fast as it left.
Remedies include saving boom revenues abroad in a sovereign wealth fund, running budget surpluses, and investing in education and infrastructure for lagging sectors.
It is hard to diagnose, but evidence suggests very large unexpected oil and gas discoveries do on average raise the real exchange rate and shrink lagging sectors.

definition.text: The classic 1982 economic model of Dutch disease, with a booming sector, a lagging tradable sector and a non-tradable services sector.

facts.text: In the resource movement effect, the boom pulls labour into the booming sector, called direct deindustrialisation.
In the spending effect, extra revenue raises demand for services, pulling labour from the lagging sector (indirect deindustrialisation) and raising the real exchange rate.
The spending effect is usually seen as the main channel, because extraction is capital-intensive and employs few workers.
